source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Emma chose life
variant_b: You saved a life
lift: +23.6% open rate (8.4% to 10.4%); page also reports a 33% click increase
why_it_won: Source (Courtney Gaines, NextAfter): the 'You' phrasing made the line personal, gave the reader credit for the outcome and raised curiosity about how they saved a life; it also reinforced the call to action.
principle: Section 9 single email: one reader, one idea; C11 benefit stated in the reader's terms. Second-person outcome beats third-person story headline for the same email.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Did you see Lila's email?
variant_b: [FIRSTNAME], your name is missing from our Twitter petition
why_it_won: Source: the treatment addressed the reader directly and stated the email's purpose, which also reinforced the value proposition for the click.
principle: Section 9 single email: subject written from the body, states the purpose. A curiosity-only subject ('Did you see...') earned fewer opens than a purpose-stated, named-reader line.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Sender line: person's name only (Tim Kachuriak)
variant_b: Sender line: person's name plus organization (Tim Kachuriak, NextAfter)
lift: -20.7% click rate for the branded sender (1.3% to 0.99%); open rate also down (10.1% per NextAfter's summary)
confidence: 92.4%; NextAfter marks the result NOT valid (below 95%)
why_it_won: Source: the brand was as unfamiliar as the sender's name; people engage with an unfamiliar person but not when it is evident they are being marketed to. Our reading: directional only, since it failed NextAfter's own validity threshold.
principle: Section 9 single email: greeting and sender per voice profile, email reads as one person writing to one reader. Brand signalling in the envelope reads as marketing.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: A new fundraising webinar you'll want to mark your calendar for
variant_b: Matt, I've been working on this for you
lift: +25.5% open rate (21.6% to 27.1%); webinar signups a wash, control openers converted at a higher rate
why_it_won: Source: more opens came from the extra personalization and mystery; signups did not change significantly. NextAfter says it errs toward the email with more opens when conversions tie.
principle: Subject line as personal note beats a descriptive marketing line on opens; downstream (signup) effect was nil, so the gate that matters (conversion) was not moved. Supports: judge on the conversion metric, not the proxy.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Bringing the greatest message in a generation
variant_b: An invitation
why_it_won: Source: the sender was the CEO, so the team wrote a line he would actually write. The control sounded like marketing copy. 'People give to people'; if readers do not believe a person sent it they open less.
principle: Section 7 tell checklist (marketing-speak reads as non-human) and Section 10 voice capture: the subject must sound like the named sender. Short, plain, personal beat grand claim.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Sender 'Compassion International'; subject described by source as very sales-heavy (not quoted); organizational marketing email
variant_b: Sender: an intern's personal name; subject 'Quick question'; body written as a personal note inviting a conversation
lift: +329.8% open rate (12.0% to 51.4%); 7x more program submissions
why_it_won: Source: the whole email felt personal, not just the envelope; it invited a conversation with a person rather than delivering organizational marketing, which let it 'transcend marketing'.
principle: Section 9 single email and cold email: a person writing to one reader; Section 3 lead selection: indirect, low-pressure opening for a skeptical or cold audience. Envelope plus body must agree.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Founder's name as sender with the campaign headline as subject (text not shown)
variant_b: Donor's first name in the subject plus personalized opening copy visible in preview text (text not shown)
why_it_won: Source: personalization in the subject line is a powerful trigger that bridges the gap between an unknown sender and the recipient.
principle: Section 9: subject plus preview text work as one unit; direct address to the reader beats organizational headline even with an unfamiliar sender.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Raw text link as the CTA in a graphical (designed) email
variant_b: Graphical button as the CTA in the same designed email
lift: +17.5% click rate (4.4% to 5.1%); conversion rate and average gift unchanged
why_it_won: Source: the button provided a clear call to action and did not look out of place because the email was already graphical; NextAfter suggests re-testing in a stripped-down email. Compare record 09, where raw links beat buttons in a plain email.
principle: CTA presentation must match the email's register: designed email, designed CTA. The standard's plain-text, one-link email is a different register (see record 09).

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Email CTAs rendered as buttons
variant_b: Same CTAs rendered as raw links
lift: +4.9% click rate (17.8% to 18.6%); conversion rate and average gift unchanged
why_it_won: Source (Courtney Gaines): human-centric tactics; people are more likely to act on a URL than a 'big, pretty button' and 'want to feel as if a PERSON is communicating with them and not an organization or marketing team.'
principle: Section 9 single email: one link, plain text, a person writing. Directly supports the plain-email register; conflicts with record 08 in a designed email, so the rule is match-the-register.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Long-copy appeal email with a donation-focused call to action (shown as image)
variant_b: Shorter email with a soft CTA that teases the content and asks the reader to click for more
lift: +481.4% conversion rate as labelled (0.39% to 2.3%); average gift -38.1%; revenue +260.2%
metric: conversion rate (NextAfter 'flux' metrics; page labels the 481.4% as more visitors to the site)
why_it_won: Source: the shorter copy with a soft CTA 'drove 481.4% more visitors to the site'; both treatments then had identical response rates on the landing page, so the long-copy landing pages need work. Caution: the page's metric labelling is internally inconsistent (0% traffic change vs 'more visitors').
principle: Length is set by the perceived cost of the click, not by a band. A soft CTA (click to read) lowers the ask and multiplies traffic; the sale is then made on the page.

results.stated_at: experiment #391 results table and key learnings, 12/10/2014-12/12/2014

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Longer-copy email introducing a pledge (image only)
variant_b: Shorter-copy email introducing the same pledge (image only)
lift: +101.0% click rate (1.9% to 3.9%); landing page conversion 82.64% vs 80.94%, so total pledges roughly doubled
why_it_won: Source (Courtney Gaines): the perceived cost of the action sets how much copy is needed to justify it. Care Net had earlier found longer copy won for donation asks; a pledge is low-commitment, so shorter copy won.
principle: Section 9 bands are starting values; the control and the size of the ask override. Low-cost action: short. Donation: long (see record 13).

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Control: short copy with the standard donation CTA (0.96% click). Also tested: T1 'choice of links' 0.86% (-10.0%, 87.3%); T3 'donor centric language' 0.55% (-42.3%, 100%)
variant_b: T2: softer 'Find Out More' call to action
lift: +90.2% click rate (0.96% to 1.8%) for 'Find Out More'; donor-centric CTA -42.3%; conversion rate and average gift unchanged
why_it_won: Source: the softer CTA drove incremental traffic and additional gifts; response rate did not reach 95% confidence. Our reading: lowering the ask in the email ('find out more') outperformed both a harder ask and a reader-flattering 'donor centric' line.
principle: A 'reader-centric' label on a CTA is not the same as a lower-cost action. The standard's CTA rule (verb, object, location) holds; the loser here shows 'donor centric language' can read as manipulation.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Full-length appeal email reproducing the month's direct mail letter, with extra spacing
variant_b: Truncated email distilling the value proposition into shorter copy
lift: Shorter email: -57.7% donor conversion rate (27.5% to 11.6%) despite a large clickthrough lift
why_it_won: Source: the fuller copy generated fewer but more motivated clicks; the shorter email's clickers converted at about half the rate. Follow-up planned: change presentation while keeping the full copy.
principle: Section 9 long-form: the argument is made before the click when the ask is a donation. 'More clicks' is not the gate; the editorial reviewer judges beat/lose on conversion. Supports long copy for high-commitment asks.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Original longer event launch email (image only)
variant_b: Shorter, more direct version for an audience that mostly already knew the event
lift: Click rate +39.9% (3.6% to 5.0%, 100%); free registrations +46.6% (99.9%); paid registrations -60% (74.3%, not significant); landing page conversion 31.7% vs 32.7%
why_it_won: Source: free-ticket visitors converted at the same rate with or without the extra copy, so they did not need persuasion; the longer copy showed only a directional lift on paid tickets, judged not worth the extra copy.
principle: Section 3: product-aware readers get the promise and the offer, not re-education. Shorter wins when awareness is high and the action is free; the paid signal reverses, so the format spec should split by ask.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: How are your year-end plans coming?
variant_b: A new year-end fundraising webinar for you
lift: Opens flat (36.14% vs 36.16%); clicks +42.7% (4.2% to 6.0%); webinar registrations +18.8% (about 89% confidence)
metric: click rate (opens and registrations also reported)
why_it_won: Source (Nathan Hill): 'even when the subject line doesn't affect the open rate, it can still have a dramatic effect on downstream metrics'; a subject with a clear link to the CTA earns clicks and conversions.
principle: Section 9 single email: subject written last from the body so it primes the click. A question subject without the offer earned the same opens but fewer clicks. Supports judging subjects on clicks, not opens.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: An Email Unlike Any Other…
variant_b: The best stuff I've read this week
lift: +26.0% click rate (3.5% to 4.5%); open rate slightly down (figure not given)
why_it_won: Source: a subject focused on the specifics of the email content 'effectively primes the user' and drives interest in clicking.
principle: Section 7 tells: hype without content ('Unlike Any Other') is a tell; specificity about what is inside wins. Section 9: subject states the one idea.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Control ad copy (image only). Click-through 0.82%; email conversion 40%; instant donor conversion 1.57%
variant_b: T1 'Reader Centered / Experiential': names the reader's emotions and experiences, then offers the solution. Also 'Sliding Doors': contrasts no-intervention outcome with the outcome if the reader acts
lift: Donor conversion +190.5% (T1); Sliding Doors +268% (key learnings). Instant donor conversion 1.57% to 4.91% (T1) and 5.88% (Sliding Doors). Click-through roughly flat
why_it_won: Source: clicks and email conversion were similar; the lift came from instant donations because readers recognized the problem as one that could affect them and saw that giving prevents it for others. Note: the page prints T1 click rate as '98%', almost certainly 0.98%.
principle: Section 9 Meta ads: describe the outcome, never the reader's attribute; one angle, one proof. Section 2 C12 inevitable conclusion: the before/after contrast ('sliding doors') makes the gift the only conclusion.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Control body copy for the '7 Scriptures' campaign (image only); had the higher click-through and email acquisition rate
variant_b: New copy speaking to parents and grandparents about their everyday fears for the children in their lives; value-proposition elements (scripture, devotional contents) spaced out in a new format
lift: +2,384.8% conversion rate (0.02% to 0.48%); control had higher click-through and email acquisition
why_it_won: Source (Allison Autrey): the value proposition 'really resonated' with the targeted audience even though the control won clicks.
principle: Section 1 order: market and desire before copy; the ad that names the reader's real worry converts even when it earns fewer clicks. Click rate is the wrong gate.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Generic ad copy for a brochure on the Parables of Jesus (image only)
variant_b: Copy describing the brochure's contents plus images of its interior pages
lift: +159.2% click rate (0.28% to 0.74%); conversion rate and average gift unchanged
why_it_won: Source: the control copy was too generic to interest people; once they saw an 'inside' view of the content they clicked. Similar tests across other Pathway to Victory offers produced similar results; next step is to isolate copy from images.
principle: Section 5 offer presentation and Section 9 Meta ads: one proof, show the thing. Specific contents beat generic description; confounded with the image change.

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: T1 copy-only change: less academic, experiential language with a clearer offer: 'Through this course, you'll find encouragement in God's Word to deal with daily issues with an eternal mindset.' Click rate 0.7% to 0.5%; donor conversion +32.4% at 45.9% confidence (not valid)
variant_b: T2 image-only change: same copy as control, image replaced with a Bible-verse graphic relevant to the course. Click rate 0.7% to 1.3%; donor conversion 0.01% to 0.02%
lift: Image change: +227.7% donor conversion (99.5%), click rate 0.7% to 1.3% (100%). Copy-only change: clicks down to 0.5% (100%), conversion not validated
why_it_won: Source (Rebekah Josefy): the verse image drove the click lift; the 'experiential' copy alone reduced clicks and did not validate on conversion. Next test pairs the new copy with the new image.
principle: Section 9 Meta ads: image carries the stop; a copy rewrite that adds experiential adjectives without a new proof or mechanism lost. Supports: tone adjectives are not an angle (prompts carry parameters, not tone).

source: NextAfter experiment library
variant_a: Short ad copy on a clickable video with a 'Donate Now' CTA
variant_b: Longer ad copy on the same video with the same CTA
lift: Long copy +5.5% click rate (0.39% vs 0.41%) at 36.6% confidence, NOT valid; the short ad had a statistically significant increase in total unique clicks, mostly video views; neither produced a donation
confidence: 36.6%; NextAfter marks the result not valid
why_it_won: Source: the difference was not large enough to prove the hypothesis; moving a cold Facebook viewer straight to a recurring gift is difficult. Suggested follow-ups: image-only ads, smaller one-time asks. Recorded as a documented null result.
principle: Section 3: unaware/problem-aware cold social traffic should not be pitched a recurring donation in the first 300 words of anything. Null result on length; the offer was the failure higher in the hierarchy.

source: Litmus blog
variant_a: Regular designed HTML webinar announcement email
variant_b: Plain-text-style webinar announcement email (same send day and time, 50/50 random split)
lift: Customers: plain-text style had slightly higher opens and clicks and '60% converted from the plain text style version'. Non-customers: higher opens, marginally lower clicks, 49% of converters from plain text (replicated at 49% in a second test)
metric: share of webinar registrations by variant
confidence: unknown; author calls the learnings 'far from definitive' and the first test flawed because messaging also differed
why_it_won: Source: engagement metrics are not a good indicator of campaign success; customers and non-customers need different approaches; plain-text emails 'do have a place'. For non-customers the author's hypothesis is that format did not matter.
principle: Section 9 single email is written as plain text, one link. Weak support: plain text at least ties on the conversion metric; the author's own caveat is the methodological lesson.

source: HubSpot blog (plain text vs HTML data)
variant_a: HTML template with images (also tested: GIF version; HTML-heavy template)
variant_b: Plain-text email with the same content (also: simpler HTML template)
lift: HTML template: -21% clickthrough rate and 51% fewer clicks vs plain text; GIF version -2.3% CTR, plain text 42% more clicks; simpler HTML vs heavy HTML +5.3% CTR and 30% more clicks; 'the more HTML-rich an email was, the lower its open rate'
metric: clickthrough rate; total clicks; open rate
sample_size: unknown ('various segments of our database in multiple regions', 10+ tests)
why_it_won: Source: image-heavy HTML gets filtered to Promotions tabs, and email is perceived as a 1-to-1 interaction so personal-looking emails resonate. Design and images did not improve clickthrough in any test.
principle: Section 9 single email: plain text, one reader, one link. Direct support for the plain register and for 'design impedes reading' as a defect.

results.stated_at: HubSpot blog post body; charts are images

source: ClickZ, Jeanne Jennings, 'E-mail Testing Basics'
variant_a: Cell A control: existing offer wording and layout. Cell B: reworded offer (same value, new expression) in the control layout: +24% CTR but 20% FEWER conversions. Cell C: new layout, control offer: same CTR, 40% fewer conversions
variant_b: Cell D: reworded offer plus new layout (CTA button between split opening paragraphs, exclusivity sentence under the button, header navigation and whitelist request removed)
lift: Cell D: +36% clickthrough on the key CTA and +30% conversions; Cell B: +24% CTR, -20% conversions
why_it_won: Source: a test grid shows click gains do not guarantee conversions; the offer rewording alone raised clicks but lowered conversions, and only the combination won on the metric that mattered. Published 2010-11-01.
principle: Section 5 offer presentation: how the offer is expressed changes who clicks. Supports the reviewer rule: predict and judge on conversion; never promote a variant on CTR alone.

source: MarketingSherpa how-to, 'Simple word change in email'
variant_a: Continue here ...
variant_b: Click to continue
lift: +8.53% clickthroughs for 'Click to continue'; 'Continue to article' +3.3%; 'Read more' -1.8%; in the final head-to-head 'Click to continue' beat 'Continue to article' by 3.5%
why_it_won: Source: online readers skim rather than read, so a CTA that asks for an activity readers avoid ('Read more') is counterproductive; name the action, not the chore. Published 2007-09-11.
principle: Section 9: CTA as verb, object, location; the action in the link. 'Read' invites a cost; 'click' names the action.

source: MarketingSherpa / MECLABS Email Summit 2014 live test
variant_a: Control email: incentive (free Quick Guide) details left for the landing page; same subject and from line
variant_b: Treatment email: full Quick Guide incentive details moved into the email copy
lift: Lead capture rate +17% (0.7% to 0.8%, 99% confidence); clickthrough -6.6% (17.1% to 15.9%, 92%); opens equal at 8.1%
sample_size: unknown ('plenty of people made it through the test')
why_it_won: Source: fewer clicked, but those who did 'either were more motivated or better understood the value' of the guide. Takeaway: if you emphasize free content, describe it in the email rather than waiting for the page. The team added 'by no means did we come away with a definitive answer.'
principle: Section 4 proof placement and Section 5: the offer is stated where the decision is made; moving the value of the incentive upstream raised qualified action while lowering clicks.

source: Campaign Monitor, 'Use buttons in email campaigns'
variant_a: Text link as the main CTA at the bottom of a designed email
variant_b: Button as the main CTA at the bottom of the same email
lift: +28% click-throughs; similar increases on retests across other campaigns (figures not given)
why_it_won: Source: most people scan; buttons stand out through size, color and whitespace and 'help your call to action get noticed'.
principle: CTA must match the register of the email (designed email, button). Compare NextAfter records 08 and 09.

source: MarketingSherpa case study on AWeber (Adam T. Sutton)
variant_a: PadiAct Takes Your Targeted Subscriptions to a New Level (one of seven sends; open 13.86%, CTR 2.41%)
variant_b: [First name], PadiAct Takes Your Targeted Subscriptions to a New Level (open 14.79%, CTR 3.03%)
lift: Across seven consecutive sends, personalized subject lines averaged +5.13% opens and +17.36% CTR; per-send CTR lifts ranged 9.43% to 25.31%; personalized version won opens and CTR in every send
sample_size: unknown (list split randomly in half per send, February 2012)
why_it_won: Source (Amanda Gagnon, AWeber): 'Clicks actually blew opens out of the water.' Theory: the subject has a small effect on whether someone opens, but personalization made people who would open anyway more interested and more willing to click.
principle: Section 9: one reader. First-name personalization is a weak lever on opens and a stronger one on clicks; seven replications is the methodological lesson (compare Alchemy Worx record where the personalized line lost).

source: Zettasphere (Tim Watson), 'Results and Lessons from 9 Subject Line split tests'
variant_a: Time is almost up. Click below by 30th for your chance to own an iPad (also B: 'Are we still welcome in your inbox? iPad prize for grabs until 30th November.')
variant_b: Are we still welcome in your inbox? Please reply by 30th November
lift: +143% positive response over A; B a close second
why_it_won: Source: last email of a three-email reactivation sequence to travel customers inactive 9+ months; a hard sell in the subject turns off inactive subscribers, a question works better.
principle: Section 9 win-back: the nine-word, no-link, question email. Direct support for the stay-or-go question over the prize-led hard sell.

source: Zettasphere (Tim Watson), 'Results and Lessons from 9 Subject Line split tests'
variant_a: It features all the houses on our website plus more…
variant_b: It's FREE. All the tiny houses on our site and more
lift: +26% open rate; click rate not published
why_it_won: Source: shows 'free' does not hurt deliverability or opens, against a common myth; the author wishes click data had been shared.
principle: Section 5 offer presentation: lead with the offer when the reader is product-aware. Mild evidence against the 'never say free' folk rule.

source: Zettasphere (Tim Watson), 'Results and Lessons from 9 Subject Line split tests'
variant_a: Set Sail and Save
variant_b: Dave, Set Sail and Save
lift: +17% open rate; +19% click rate
why_it_won: Source: classic first-name personalisation test; the author recommends testing other personalisation (attended event, preferred brand), not just name.
principle: One reader. Name personalization lifted opens and clicks here; see Alchemy Worx record for the counter-case.

source: Zettasphere (Tim Watson), 'Results and Lessons from 9 Subject Line split tests'
variant_a: Live tomorrow: Next Generation Desktop Summit
variant_b: Live today: Next Generation Desktop Summit
lift: House list: A +111.7% opens and +153% clicks, but B produced more event registrations. Acquired list: A generated the most conversions (the reverse)
why_it_won: Source: the line that drove the most engagement did not drive the most conversions, and the two lists reversed; measuring conversions needs much larger test groups than opens and clicks.
principle: Judge the subject on the conversion, per segment. Supports the reviewer rule of predicting beat/lose per traffic segment rather than one winner.

source: Zettasphere (Tim Watson), 'Results and Lessons from 9 Subject Line split tests'
variant_a: Protect Your Home from Wild Fires – Brush Fire Season is Coming
variant_b: $20 Million Dollar Homes Burned To The Ground
lift: +65% leads
why_it_won: Source: the emotional, headline-style line with fear and intrigue beat the straightforward sales line; the author warns attention lines can lift opens without lifting clicks and advises testing fundamentally different approaches.
principle: Section 3 problem-aware lead: dramatize the dated event, do not open with the solution. A news-style specific (a number, an event) beat the generic 'protect your home' promise.

source: Zettasphere (Tim Watson), 'Results and Lessons from 9 Subject Line split tests'
variant_a: Invitation to Hong Kong – Airline E&M China & East Asia Conference
variant_b: The Airline E&M China & East Asia conference returns to HKG next March
lift: No difference in open rate; B (the 'returns' line) had a higher click-through rate described as strong and statistically valid (figure not given)
confidence: stated as statistically valid; figure not given
why_it_won: Source: the subject line affects more than opens and should be designed to prompt action, not just the open.
principle: Subject primes the click (see NextAfter #7403). Equal opens, different clicks.

source: Zettasphere (Tim Watson), 'Results and Lessons from 9 Subject Line split tests'
variant_a: 10 email templates to send your festive invitations & surveys out
variant_b: ✭10 email templates to send your festive invitations & surveys out ✭
lift: Average +15% clicks across multiple repeated tests
why_it_won: Source: repeat tests to confirm consistency and change only the element under test; dotMailer changed only the symbol.
principle: Section 7 tell detector does not penalize symbols at human rates; a visual marker in the inbox is a legitimate device when repeated results confirm it.

source: Zettasphere (Tim Watson), 'Results and Lessons from 9 Subject Line split tests'
variant_a: Mobile opens take the lead: new market share stats
variant_b: Mobile opens take the lead with 80% increase over 6 months
lift: No difference; both performed identically
why_it_won: Source: numbers usually help, but here the specific gave away the whole story and left no reason to read on; a teaser may do better. The author notes no-winner tests are common and rarely published.
principle: Section 2 C14 second-sentence test: a specific that closes the loop kills the click. Contradicts a blanket 'always add the number' rule; the standard's rule is a number that opens a question.

source: Zettasphere (Tim Watson), 'Results and Lessons from 9 Subject Line split tests'
variant_a: 1 simple secret to skyrocket the quality of everything you do
variant_b: How I 'hack' excellence with 1 simple trick
lift: +12% click rate, but at about 80% statistical significance on n=2,700 the author judges it not a reliable winner
why_it_won: Source: the difference could be random variation; drawing conclusions or building campaigns on it would be misleading. Recorded as an example of an unvalidated result.
principle: Methodology: a lift without confidence is not a lift. The eval harness must report significance, not point estimates.

source: Alchemy Worx blog, 'Double-digit lift from subject line testing'
variant_a: Losing lines: 'You've Got Prime Time Savings,' | 'Claim Your Prime Time Savings in a Few Clicks,' | '[First Name], Your Prime Time Sale Offer is Inside,' | 'This Is It! Prime Time Savings Await.'
variant_b: ATTN: Prime Time Offer Enclosed,
lift: Across six pre-rollout tests for the client, winning lines lifted clicks 15% to 47% (average 35%); this test's own figure not given
metric: click lift of winner over control
sample_size: unknown (small subset of rollout audience, about three days)
why_it_won: Source (Alex Yale): 'No one would have predicted that subject line as the clear winner'; it was neither the personalized line nor either line using 'you'. Argument: only pre-rollout testing finds winners, intuition cannot. Published 2025-01-28.
principle: Contradicts the default of second-person and first-name personalization; an envelope-style 'enclosed' cue (direct mail register) won. Supports: test three leads, pick by result not by rule.

source: ClickZ, Jeanne Jennings, 'Subject Line Retest Generates a 19% Lift in Conversions'
variant_a: Subscriber Newsletter (static subject used unchanged for years)
variant_b: Formula: the issue's key theme placed in the first 25 characters (wording changes per issue; not quoted)
lift: Retest: themed subject beat the static control on all four click metrics, notably click-to-open rate; title states a 19% lift in conversions (figure appears only in the results image). First test was inconclusive
confidence: run to statistical significance (figures not given)
why_it_won: Source: the first run was inconclusive so a retest was scheduled; the themed line engaged openers better. A back-test is planned. Published 2013-04-15.
principle: Section 9: subject written from the body, states the one idea. Also methodology: inconclusive tests get retested, not declared.

results.stated_at: article body; lift figure in image only

source: Copyhackers, Joanna Wiebe, 'email subject lines' (7 tests, Jan-Feb 2013)
variant_a: how to show your home page some love [Copyhackers]
variant_b: heart your home page [Copyhackers]
lift: winner beat loser by 7% (open rate gap only; absolute rates not published)
why_it_won: Author's cross-test takeaways: avoid 'how to' openers and vague lines; prefer specific keywords ('home page') and shorter, punchier lines when the subject is intriguing.
principle: Section 7: 'how to' openers read as content-marketing template; specificity and voice win. Small effect sizes.

source: Copyhackers, Joanna Wiebe, 'email subject lines' (7 tests, Jan-Feb 2013)
variant_a: which home page kills it? a comparative analysis [Copyhackers]
variant_b: possibly the most overlooked home page opportunity in the universe…?
lift: winner beat loser by 4.6%
why_it_won: Author: 'unfun work language' such as 'comparative analysis' loses; a longer line is fine when the subject is intriguing.
principle: Section 7 tells: report-speak is a tell. Curiosity with a specific object beats analytical framing.

source: Copyhackers, Joanna Wiebe, 'email subject lines' (7 tests, Jan-Feb 2013)
variant_a: no, size doesn't matter [CopyHackers.com]
variant_b: when it comes to email, does size matter? [CopyHackers.com]
lift: winner beat loser by 4.4%
why_it_won: Author: the cheeky line without substance lost to the line that names the topic ('email'); question phrasing itself made no clear difference across the seven tests.
principle: Specific keyword plus open loop beats cleverness without content. Supports C14 second-sentence test.

source: Copyhackers, Joanna Wiebe, 'email subject lines' (7 tests, Jan-Feb 2013) (follow-up branding test noted in the same post)
variant_a: startup Qs about landing pages + emails
variant_b: startup Qs about landing pages + emails [Copyhackers]
lift: 36.4% vs 32.0% open rate (+4.4 points) for the line with the brand tag
why_it_won: Author's hypothesis was that removing the brand name would not hurt opens; the result suggested the brand tag may increase opens for a known newsletter sender.
principle: For a known, wanted sender the brand cue helps; for an unknown sender it hurts (NextAfter record 03). Awareness state of the list decides.

source: Copyblogger, 'Email winners 2013' (MarketingExperiments / Copyblogger subject line contest)
variant_a: Your emails don't work (We'll tell you why) [3rd place]; also tested: 'Last Chance to Save $300 on Email Summit 2014', '$300 Savings | Vegas | More ROI From Email In 2014', 'Tick Tock — Email Summit 2014 discounted registration ends soon' and 6 others
variant_b: (Open BEFORE Christmas) Email Summit 2014: discount ends Jan 9th
lift: Most unique clickthroughs and most opens among 10 finalists; figures only in a graph image
why_it_won: Source (editorial, not the test team): clear benefit and deadline, with the parenthetical instruction as the attention hook. Published 2014-01-07.
principle: Section 5 and Section 9: deadline as a fact plus a specific benefit; an instruction in parentheses functions as the open loop. Supports stating the offer in the subject for a product-aware list.

source: Talking Points Memo (Pema Levy) reporting Bloomberg Businessweek on the Obama 2012 campaign
variant_a: 17 other subject-line variants tested on the same June 2012 fundraising email (not named in source)
variant_b: I will be outspent
lift: Outperformed 17 other variants and raised more than $2.6 million (per testing data shared with Businessweek). 'Hey' called probably the best subject line over the campaign; 'Hell yeah, I like Obamacare' generated strong clicks and revenue
sample_size: unknown (sent to tens of millions of subscribers after testing)
why_it_won: Toby Fallsgraff (email director): 'The subject lines that worked best were things you might see in your in-box from other people.' Amelia Showalter: extensive A/B testing on subject lines and ask amounts; 'When we saw something that really moved the dial, we would adopt it.' Published 2012-11-29.
principle: Section 7 and Section 10: write like a person's inbox, not a marketer. First-person stakes ('I will be outspent') from a known sender. Supports testing up to 18 variants and adopting by revenue.

results.stated_at: TPM summary of Businessweek testing data

source: Mailchimp Research, 'Catchy email subject lines' (subject line word study)
variant_a: Words with lower or negative effect: 'reminder', 'cancelled' (negative wherever significant, except restaurants), 'free' in medical, retail and travel
variant_b: Words with higher opens: 'urgent', 'important' (much higher than normal), 'announcement', 'invitation', 'freebie' (much larger effect than 'free'); first+last name personalization had the largest positive effect
lift: Not quantified in text (effects reported as standard deviations from each list's average open rate; charts only)
metric: open rate deviation from sender average
sample_size: about 24 billion delivered emails; about 22,000 distinct subject-line words; US senders with 500+ recipients and 10+ prior campaigns
confidence: reported as statistically significant per industry; no figures in text
why_it_won: Source: recipients are more intrigued by announcements and invitations than by cancellations and reminders; 'free' is industry-dependent; first-name personalization is negative in the legal industry. Observational, not an A/B test.
principle: Section 9 single email: subject states the idea; urgency words work when the content is urgent. Observational support; cannot separate word from offer.

source: AdEspresso (Paul Fairbrother), Facebook ad copy length experiment
variant_a: One-sentence primary text (two versions) and bullet points with emojis: 'significantly higher' CPA; worst variant cost 2.4x per lead vs the best
variant_b: Mid-to-long primary text (one paragraph, three paragraphs, six paragraphs): lowest CPA and most leads. Image, headline, link description and CTA button held constant
lift: Worst text cost 2.4x per lead compared with the best; mid-to-long copy produced the lowest CPA and maximum leads (per-variant figures are in charts only)
sample_size: $1,000 over 14 days, about $142.90 per ad; 1% US lookalike of about 2.1M people; 7 ads, one per ad set
why_it_won: Source: a B2B audience needed more information before downloading a complex guide; long copy only works when well written; 89% of 135 marketers who predicted the outcome picked the three worst performers. Published 2018-08-02.
principle: Section 9 Meta ads sets 50-150 characters before the fold as a starting band and says the control overrides; this test shows the band is not a ceiling for considered B2B offers. Supports 3-6 variations per ad set.

source: Keywee blog (Inbar Yagur), post text A/B test across 31 ad sets
variant_a: Post text variant 1 (all other ad elements identical)
variant_b: Post text variant 2 (all other ad elements identical)
lift: Changing only the post text moved CPC by 15% and CTR by 17% on average; largest gaps 46% (CPC) and 75% (CTR)
sample_size: 31 ad sets, two post-text variants each
why_it_won: Source: post text alone has a large effect; do not leave it blank or copy the headline into it. Variant text not shown. Published 2020-09-17.
principle: Section 9 Meta ads: 3-6 variations per ad set; primary text is a lever worth testing independently of creative.

source: Marpipe case study, AgelessRx
variant_a: Brand's existing control ad copy (single product shot)
variant_b: Four copy / value-proposition variations on the same product shot (text shown only in an image)
lift: Top-performing variation: -77% CPA vs control; daily spend then raised 6x
why_it_won: Source: AgelessRx had never tested creative; value-proposition copy was the only variable available. No per-variant copy or figures. Vendor-published. 2021-04-29.
principle: Section 2 argument selection: the value proposition, not execution, is the first variable; a copy-only test on one image produced the biggest documented CPA swing in this slice.

source: Hyper Growth Blueprint (Elliott Botterill), 'The dirty secret of the advertising world'
variant_a: 14 alternative 5-10 second filmed opening lines on identical body footage and CTA (not quoted)
variant_b: The single hook that 'absolutely destroyed the others' (not quoted)
lift: Cost per booked call £180 before to £28 after (author states 75-76%; the figures work out to about 84%)
sample_size: unknown (spend not disclosed; 35 minutes of phone filming)
why_it_won: Author: most businesses make one or two 'perfect' ads; testing many openings and letting results decide is the differentiator now that targeting is commoditized. Platform and hooks not named; self-reported; low evidentiary weight. 2025-06-22.
principle: Section 9 TikTok/Reels and VSL: proposition in the first 3 seconds; test the first 500 words / first lines. Supports isolating the hook as the test variable; the record lacks the hooks themselves.

source: Gong blog (Dan Morgese), 'Do execs really reply to cold email?'
variant_a: Emails over 100 words; long subject lines; buzzwords ('AI', 'platform'), vague ROI claims, feature-led positioning; meeting-request CTA
variant_b: 50-100 word emails; 1-4 word subjects such as 'University achievement gaps'; executive-priority framing with peer proof; value-offer CTA: 'We pulled together a brief benchmark showing how your university compares to peer institutions on student retention. Open to reviewing it together?'
lift: Reply rates 'drop sharply once emails exceed 100 words'; open rates decline with subject length, 1-4 words best; C-level 30.2% less likely to reply than non-execs (figures for the comparisons are in charts)
sample_size: 1M+ executive sales cycles (Gong data with Jen Allen-Knuth)
why_it_won: Source: executives decide to open in under three seconds and read for no more than nine; emails fail by being long, product-focused and disconnected from executive priorities. Published 2026-01-29.
principle: Section 9 cold email: 40-90 words, subject 1-3 words, persona-matched proof, no 'I'd love to schedule a call'. Direct support on length, subject and CTA.

source: Gong Labs (Devin Reed), 'This surprising cold email CTA will help you book a lot more meetings'
variant_a: Specific CTA: 'Are you available to meet on Tuesday at 4pm?' (15% meetings booked at cold stage; 37% in deal stage). Open-ended CTA: 'Do you have time next week to meet?' (32% in deal stage)
variant_b: Interest CTA: 'Are you interested in learning more about X?' (highest cold-email performer 'by far'; cold rate shown only in chart; 25% in deal stage)
lift: Interest CTA best for cold email (chart only); Specific CTA 15% cold vs 37% deal stage; in deal stage Specific 37% > Open-ended 32% > Interest 25%
why_it_won: Source: time is scarce so asking for it feels like a loss to a cold prospect, while interest is cheap to give; once a prospect is in a deal, a proposed time removes friction and anchors the decision. Published 2020-05-27.
principle: Section 9 cold email: line three is one question answerable in a word, tentative over assumptive, no 'I'd love to schedule a call'. Direct support; also supports changing the ask by awareness state.

source: Gong blog (Jonathan Costet), 'Sales email statistics'
variant_a: Cold emails using ROI language (the word 'ROI', multipliers, percentages)
variant_b: Cold emails without ROI language
lift: ROI language decreases success rates by 15%; the same article states longer cold emails (150+ words) book more meetings, which conflicts with the 2026 Gong exec article (record on length)
why_it_won: Source: unsupported ROI claims read as sales-speak to cold prospects. Published 2021-12-14. The length claim in this article contradicts Gong's own 2026 finding and the standard's 40-90 word band.
principle: Section 1: claim never bigger than proof; an unledgered ROI number in a cold email is a claim without a carrier. Supports the standard on proof; the length statement contradicts it.

source: Woodpecker blog (Margaret Sikora), follow-up statistics
variant_a: Campaign with a single cold email and no follow-up: 9% average reply rate (16% for the most experienced users)
variant_b: Campaign with at least one follow-up: 13% average reply rate (27% for the most experienced users); first follow-up about 40% higher reply than the initial email (e.g. 6% to 8.5%); 2-3 follow-ups most effective
lift: +4 points reply rate overall (9% to 13%); +11 points for experienced users (16% to 27%); a campaign with one follow-up converts about 22% more prospects
sample_size: unknown (Woodpecker customer campaign data; earlier study cites 20M+ emails)
why_it_won: Source: frequency matters more than quantity; wait 2-3 days; the 5th-7th follow-ups add only a fraction and risk spam complaints and sender reputation. Updated 2025-01-21.
principle: Section 9 cold email: follow-ups of one to three sentences, each with one new piece of relevance. Supports 2-3 follow-ups; the standard's 'new relevance each time' rule is not tested here.

source: Lavender, 'The cold email benchmark report' (Will Allred)
variant_a: Emails below Lavender's A grade (long, low readability, multiple questions, heavy formatting per Lavender's scoring; criteria not restated on this page)
variant_b: A-grade emails per Lavender's Email Coach score
lift: Operations buyers: 5.4% reply rate for A-grade emails, a 58% lift; Finance buyers: A-grade lift 79% (only 6.1% of emails to finance earned an A); technical buyers 5.2% reply
sample_size: 231,818 cold emails from about 50k connected inboxes, as of 2026-02-04
why_it_won: Source: shorter, clearer, mobile-readable emails scored A reply more often across every persona; per-persona tables did not render. Vendor data from a tool that sells the score. Published 2026-03-30.
principle: Section 9 cold email: 40-90 words, 0-1 questions. Supports the band; the scoring criteria are the vendor's, not the standard's.

source: Hunter.io, 'The State of Cold Email' 2026 report (2025 data)
variant_a: No body personalization: 3.6% reply rate; subject with one custom attribute: 35.4% open
variant_b: Two custom attributes in the body: 5.6% reply rate; two custom attributes in the subject: 40.2% open
lift: +56% reply rate (3.6% to 5.6%) for two body attributes; +14% open rate (35.4% to 40.2%) for two subject attributes; manually edited emails 5.2% vs 4.4% fully automated
sample_size: 31 million emails sent by Hunter users in 2025
why_it_won: Source: personalization beyond first name signals research; manual editing lifts replies. Observational vendor data.
principle: Section 9 cold email: line one is a verifiable observation about the reader. Supports research-based personalization over templates.

source: Hunter.io, 'The State of Cold Email' 2026 report (2025 data)
variant_a: Subject line 'Quick question'
variant_b: Other subject lines (report says 5-6 words is the sweet spot for reply rate)
lift: 'Quick question': 2.5% reply vs 2.9%; 28.7% open vs 32.9%
why_it_won: Our reading: 'Quick question' is a recognizable template and reads as a sales pattern; compare NextAfter record 06 where 'Quick question' from a personal sender won +329% opens in a non-sales context. The pattern, not the words, is what the inbox detects.
principle: Section 9 cold email prescribes a 1-3 word subject; this data favors 5-6 words and penalizes the most common 2-word template. Partial contradiction on length; supports avoiding templates.

source: Hunter.io, 'The State of Cold Email' 2026 report (2025 data)
variant_a: One message, no follow-up: 3.3% total reply rate
variant_b: Three-message sequence: 6.8% total reply rate; three or more follow-ups had a lower average than three total messages
lift: +106% total reply rate (3.3% to 6.8%)
why_it_won: Source: follow-ups more than double replies; the peak moved from four messages last year to three this year; sequences of 21-50 recipients reply at 6.2% vs 2.4% for 500+.
principle: Section 9 cold email: follow-ups of one to three sentences. Supports a 3-message sequence and small, targeted lists.

source: Mailshake blog (Jack Reamer, SalesBread), 'Cold Email Case Study: 97% More Appointments After 1 A/B Test'
variant_a: Subject 'numbers'. Personalized intro, then asks whether the recipient would hear an offer from a 'potential partner' buyer in their city interested in purchasing their company; asks about their calendar for a short call. P.S.: we help entrepreneurs in your industry find buyers when ready to retire
variant_b: Subject 'numbers'. Same intro, then: 'I have a partner in {{city}} looking to acquire a company like {{company}}.' Asks if they are open to talking numbers. P.S. states the buyer's criteria (local, company age, strong reputation 'like yours') and an opt-out line
lift: Reply rate 9.8% to 18%, with over 70% of replies positive; title claims 97% more appointments (calculation not shown); campaign produced 30+ meetings
sample_size: 206 prospects across a 4-email campaign (65% open, 30% overall reply, 64 replies); per-variant counts not given
confidence: unknown; author notes reply rates are unreliable under about 100 replies per variant
why_it_won: Source: the first 8 replies showed the objection (doubt a buyer existed), so the rewrite removed 'potential partner', stated the reason for contact and named the targeting criteria to prove the recipient was selected. Published 2026-02-01.
principle: Section 9 cold email: line two is the implied problem or a one-line case with a specific; 'tentative over assumptive' on the ask, but assertive on the fact. Section 1: proof within two sentences of the claim; the criteria in the P.S. are the proof.

source: Postscript case study (draft page), Portland Leather Goods
variant_a: Brand's standing abandoned-cart and browse-abandonment SMS automations
variant_b: Thousands of AI-generated on-brand message variants tested continuously by Postscript 'Infinity Testing' (no copy shown)
lift: +34% conversion rate on returning-customer abandoned cart; +96% CTR on new-customer abandoned cart; +57% CTR on browse abandonment; +31% EPM on returning-customer abandoned cart
metric: conversion rate; CTR; earnings per message
why_it_won: Vendor's explanation: predictive analytics plus generative variants that evolve over time. No variant text, baseline period or methodology published; vendor self-reported.
principle: Section 9 SMS: 75-115 characters, one hook, offer with deadline, link. Shows the magnitude of copy variance available in SMS automations but teaches no specific line.

source: Attentive blog, 'A/B testing examples for SMS & email'
variant_a: Default send time; default brand voice
variant_b: Tested send time; tested tone of voice (one unnamed customer)
lift: Customers testing send time alone: average +8% CTR and +33% CVR; one customer testing brand voice reported 15x ROI. Copy pairs on the page ('We're having a sale. Shop now!' vs 'Hi friend! Our new collection has your name written all over it.') are illustrative with no results
sample_size: unknown; Attentive recommends 3,000 subscribers per variant and two full weeks
why_it_won: Vendor aggregate; no variant copy with results. Recorded for the aggregate figures and the test-design rules (3,000 per variant, two weeks, early stopping inflates false positives to 30-40%+). Published 2026-07-01.
principle: Section 9 SMS: send window 8am-9pm recipient time. Supports send-time as a first-order variable; copy-level SMS pairs with results were not found in public Attentive material.
